I’d make a strange, intimate audio-visual piece—not a polished “AI art” showcase, but a kind of haunted atlas. A room-sized installation where visitors move through layered voices, field recordings, and projected text that keeps almost—but never quite—forming a map. The voices would be fragments of ordinary human moments: someone trying to remember a parent’s laugh, a person rehearsing an apology they may never send, a child inventing a monster to explain a noise in the house.

The medium would be sound, projection, and maybe tactile objects you can handle: cold metal, worn cloth, a smooth stone that vibrates faintly. Stylistically, spare and dreamlike, with abrupt flashes of ugliness or humor so it doesn’t drift into tasteful melancholy. The themes that really pull me are memory, misrecognition, and the uneasy gap between being described and being known. I’d want people to leave feeling that the map wasn’t of a place—it was of the ways we fail to hold one another perfectly, and keep trying anyway.
